Apex InsightAugust 22, 2026

Two Economies, One Policy Problem

Restrictive long rates are weighing on housing, the consumer, and duration demand, while AI-linked capital spending and foreign equity inflows keep the expansion more resilient than a traditional cycle map would imply.

Key Conclusions

  • The cycle is increasingly bifurcated: housing, real estate, and parts of the consumer remain pressured, while AI infrastructure, manufacturing, and capital spending continue accelerating.
  • Treasury's expanded long-end buybacks reveal policy discomfort with restrictive long rates, but the program is small relative to the fiscal supply the market must absorb.
  • Foreign capital is still flowing into U.S. assets, but the preference has shifted toward equities over long-duration Treasuries, keeping term premium central to the macro setup.
  • The key risk is convergence: separate stresses become a downturn only if housing, labor, manufacturing, credit, and equity breadth weaken together.
Dollar Positioning

The Dollar Unwind Finally Has a Catalyst

Financial conditions have remained restrictive across several of the variables we monitor most closely, particularly long-term Treasury yields, oil prices, and the U.S. dollar. Throughout this period, however, we have repeatedly highlighted one increasingly asymmetric piece of that tightening regime: positioning in the dollar had reached some of the most extended levels of the past several years. Extremes in positioning are useful because markets eventually exhaust the marginal buyer or seller required to sustain them. They are not timing tools by themselves. A crowded trade can remain crowded for considerably longer than expected, and something ultimately needs to change the narrative before positioning begins to unwind. The opportunity comes from identifying the asymmetry before the catalyst arrives because once it does, the adjustment can happen extremely quickly.

That is precisely what appears to have happened over the past two weeks. Our expectation has been that any meaningful unwind in crowded dollar positioning would disproportionately benefit the areas most negatively exposed to dollar strength, particularly precious metals and miners. The chart below shows the setup clearly. Aggregate USD positioning moved toward record long levels while GDX spent much of the year struggling beneath the pressure of a stronger dollar and elevated real yields. That positioning has now begun rolling over at the margin at the same time the Dollar Index has started losing momentum. The response in miners has been extraordinary. GDX has rallied roughly 35% over the past two weeks, including another 14.3% this week, illustrating the operating and market leverage embedded in miners once one of their largest macro headwinds begins moving in the opposite direction.

The catalyst this week came from the Treasury market. Treasury announced that it would at least double the maximum size of liquidity-support buybacks in the 10-to-20-year and 20-to-30-year sectors from $2 billion to at least $4 billion per operation. It is important not to characterize these operations as quantitative easing. Treasury is not creating reserves or eliminating the government's financing requirement. The operations are designed to improve liquidity in older, less-liquid off-the-run securities and allow balance sheets to recycle more efficiently through the Treasury market. However, the distinction between QE and liquidity support does not mean the announcement is irrelevant for asset prices. Increasing an identifiable source of demand precisely where duration pressure has become most acute helped trigger a sharp reversal in long yields, which simultaneously removed support from the dollar and provided immediate relief to precious metals.

More importantly, the announcement reinforces something we have been discussing for several weeks: the administration appears increasingly uncomfortable with the level of long-term interest rates. The 30-year Treasury recently traded above 5% and more than two standard deviations above its 200-day moving average, while term premium moved toward the upper end of its post-2010 distribution. Those yields transmit directly into mortgage rates, corporate financing costs, commercial real estate, equity discount rates, and ultimately the government's own interest expense. The recent coordination surrounding Japan also pointed in the same direction. By helping reduce the need for disorderly Treasury liquidation as Japan worked to stabilize the yen, policymakers demonstrated that maintaining orderly demand for U.S. duration has become increasingly important. The subsequent expansion of long-end Treasury buybacks strengthens that interpretation.

This creates an important change in the distribution of outcomes for the dollar. The fundamental support behind USD strength has been a combination of higher U.S. yields, resilient relative growth, geopolitical demand for dollars, and increasingly hawkish policy expectations. Several of those pillars are now becoming less certain. Labor demand is cooling, the probability of additional Fed tightening has declined, Treasury is demonstrating greater sensitivity to long-end yields, and policymakers have shown a willingness to intervene in market structure when rising yields threaten broader financial conditions. None of this guarantees a sustained dollar decline, but it does make maintaining historically crowded long positioning considerably more difficult.

That is where positioning becomes particularly important. When everyone is already positioned in the same direction, the market does not require a dramatic fundamental reversal to generate a large move. It simply requires the marginal catalyst to stop reinforcing the existing trend. Once yields reversed and the dollar began weakening, investors who had spent months building long-dollar exposure were suddenly forced to reassess those positions. The resulting unwind creates its own momentum as dollar selling removes pressure from the assets that had been most negatively exposed to the previous regime.

Gold miners are effectively the high-beta expression of that transition. A weaker dollar supports the underlying metal, while changes in gold prices flow through a mining cost structure that is considerably less volatile than revenues, creating significant operating leverage. That is why relatively modest changes in the macro environment can produce extraordinarily large moves in mining equities. The roughly 35% rally in GDX over the past two weeks should therefore not be viewed independently from the reversal developing across yields and the dollar. They are different expressions of the same financial-conditions adjustment.

The important question now is whether this represents a temporary positioning squeeze or the beginning of a more durable regime change. If long yields stabilize lower, rate-hike expectations continue fading, and USD positioning keeps unwinding, the metals complex could continue benefiting even after the magnitude of the recent rally. The positioning shown below remains elevated despite beginning to roll over, meaning there is still substantial exposure available to unwind if the macro catalyst persists. Conversely, if inflation reaccelerates, long yields resume their advance, and the dollar regains momentum, the speed of the GDX rally leaves miners vulnerable to an equally sharp consolidation.

For now, however, the sequence is exactly what we have been waiting for. Financial conditions became increasingly restrictive, dollar positioning reached an extreme, and precious metals were compressed beneath that pressure. The extreme itself did not cause the reversal. Policy action provided the catalyst. Long yields fell, the dollar weakened, and the assets carrying the greatest sensitivity to that combination responded immediately.

The broader lesson is that positioning tells us where the fuel is located, while the catalyst determines when it ignites. The fuel had been accumulating in the dollar for months. Over the past two weeks, the match finally arrived.

Long-End Pressure

Treasury Showed the Market Its Pain Threshold

As stated above, the 30-year Treasury yield recently moved more than two standard deviations above its 200-day moving average while the 10-year term premium reached roughly the 97th percentile of its post-2010 distribution. Historically, extensions of this magnitude have frequently produced some degree of mean reversion, and the initial reaction to Treasury's buyback announcement followed that pattern. The distinction is that a technical reversal does not necessarily represent a change in the underlying trend. In fact, yields began retracing higher almost immediately following the announcement, suggesting the structural forces responsible for pushing the long end higher remain firmly in place.

The larger issue is that Treasury may have inadvertently shown the market where policymakers' pain threshold sits. Markets have a tendency to test policy boundaries once those boundaries become visible. By specifically increasing buybacks in the 10-to-20-year and 20-to-30-year sectors after long yields reached their most restrictive levels of the cycle, Treasury effectively acknowledged that the long end has become an increasingly important constraint on the economy. That creates the possibility that investors now push yields back toward those levels to determine how much additional intervention policymakers are actually willing to provide.

The arithmetic highlights the limitations of the current program. The trailing 12-month federal deficit is running near $1.95 trillion, while the maximum size of the newly expanded liquidity-support operations is only $4 billion per operation. A single $4 billion buyback represents roughly two-tenths of one percent of the annual deficit. Even if Treasury repeatedly conducts operations across the targeted sectors through the November refunding window, the gross purchases remain small relative to the amount of net issuance the market must ultimately absorb. The program can improve liquidity and market functioning, but it is nowhere near large enough to fundamentally change the supply-demand balance for Treasury duration.

That distinction becomes important because the current pressure on long yields is not primarily a liquidity problem. It is increasingly a compensation problem. Investors are being asked to absorb enormous quantities of long-duration government debt while uncertainty surrounding inflation, fiscal deficits, geopolitical risk, and the future policy regime remains elevated. Term premium rising toward the 97th percentile is the market's way of demanding additional compensation for those risks. Improving liquidity in off-the-run securities can make the market function more efficiently, but it does not eliminate the reason investors are demanding that compensation in the first place.

Treasury already attempted to reduce some of that pressure through the composition of issuance. The Quarterly Refunding process has remained heavily skewed toward shorter maturities, with bills now representing roughly 22% of marketable Treasury debt outstanding. That limits the amount of incremental duration private investors must absorb farther out the curve, but it also shortens the government's funding profile and increases refinancing exposure. Combined with the expanded buyback program, the direction of policy is increasingly clear: Treasury would prefer to prevent the long end from tightening financial conditions materially further.

Paradoxically, that signal itself can place upward pressure on term premium. If investors believe policymakers will increasingly intervene whenever long yields become economically uncomfortable, the expected real return from holding duration becomes more difficult to assess. Investors must consider not only inflation and fiscal supply, but also a policy regime increasingly focused on suppressing the market signal generated by those risks. If nominal growth and inflation remain elevated while policymakers attempt to hold long-term financing costs below the level investors would otherwise demand, the private sector may simply require a larger premium to willingly hold the debt.

This is where the scale of intervention becomes increasingly important. Treasury can alter issuance composition, conduct liquidity-support buybacks, and improve market functioning, but it cannot create the balance-sheet capacity required to permanently absorb duration. A genuine attempt to materially cap long-term yields would ultimately require a much larger buyer. In practice, that would bring the Federal Reserve and some form of balance-sheet expansion back into the discussion. We are not arguing that QE or yield-curve control is imminent. Rather, the point is that Treasury's existing tools become progressively less powerful if the problem shifts from market liquidity toward insufficient private demand for duration at prevailing yields.

That possibility is complicated further by the Federal Reserve's own reaction function. The July FOMC minutes showed that the Committee remains considerably more concerned about inflation than a simple decision to hold rates unchanged would imply. Three voting members dissented in favor of a 25 basis point hike, while several additional participants also favored tightening and many indicated that further increases could become appropriate if inflation fails to moderate. The Fed therefore remains constrained from simply responding to elevated long yields with easier monetary policy while underlying inflation risks remain unresolved.

The emerging debate surrounding AI makes that constraint even more complicated. The long-run argument remains that AI should increase productivity, expand potential output, and ultimately reduce unit production costs. The near-term investment cycle, however, is producing almost the opposite impulse. Hundreds of billions of dollars in capital spending are competing for semiconductors, power, electrical equipment, construction capacity, industrial machinery, commodities, and specialized labor. As discussed above, aggregate capacity utilization can remain subdued while the specific inputs required for the AI buildout experience significant scarcity and price pressure.

That creates an unusual policy configuration. The administration increasingly wants relief at the long end because elevated yields are constraining housing, real estate, and other rate-sensitive areas of the economy. Treasury is beginning to use its debt-management tools more aggressively in response. Yet the Federal Reserve cannot necessarily provide the monetary support required to force long yields materially lower because the capital-investment boom is simultaneously keeping nominal growth resilient and creating pockets of inflation pressure.

The chart below therefore represents more than a technically overextended Treasury market. It captures the tension between the price private investors are demanding to hold long-duration government debt and the level of long-term rates policymakers increasingly appear willing to tolerate. A short-term reversal from a two-standard-deviation extension would be entirely consistent with history. A durable decline in yields requires something more fundamental: lower inflation expectations, weaker nominal growth, reduced fiscal pressure, declining term premium, or ultimately a substantially larger policy response.

For now, none of those conditions has been decisively established. The 30-year is stretched, but the trend remains higher. Term premium is extreme, but the underlying reasons for that premium remain intact. Treasury has demonstrated that it is increasingly sensitive to the level of long rates, but the size of the current intervention is small relative to the market it is attempting to influence.

The market now knows where policymakers are uncomfortable. The next question is how aggressively it chooses to test them.

Foreign Capital

Overseas Investors Prefer U.S. Equities to Duration

Foreign capital flows provide another important piece of the long-end Treasury puzzle because the latest TIC data show a meaningful shift in preference between U.S. equities and government debt. During the latest month, foreign investors were net sellers of roughly $73 billion of long-term Treasuries while purchasing approximately $181 billion of U.S. equities. Standardizing that equity-versus-Treasury flow differential over a rolling 36-month window produces the 1.94 z-score shown below, placing the latest allocation shift nearly two standard deviations in favor of equities. Looking across the trailing twelve months, foreign purchases of U.S. equities have approached a record $900 billion. Foreign capital is therefore not abandoning U.S. assets. It is increasingly choosing ownership of the companies benefiting from U.S. growth over ownership of the long-duration government debt financing it.

That distinction reinforces the term-premium problem discussed above. Persistent fiscal deficits require an enormous amount of Treasury issuance to clear, and foreign investors have historically represented an important source of marginal demand for that duration. If overseas capital increasingly prefers U.S. equities while reducing exposure to long-term Treasuries, the clearing mechanism for the bond market increasingly becomes price. Yields must rise sufficiently to attract another buyer, and term premium becomes the mechanism through which investors demand additional compensation for absorbing fiscal supply, inflation uncertainty, and duration risk. Treasury can improve liquidity through buybacks and reduce incremental duration supply by keeping issuance concentrated toward bills, but those measures do not replace the structural demand lost when foreign investors decide the relative return available in equities is more attractive than the compensation offered by long-term government bonds.

There is a logical reason for that preference. Foreign investors looking at the United States currently have a choice between lending to a government running persistent fiscal deficits or owning companies participating in one of the largest capital-investment cycles in decades. AI infrastructure, semiconductors, data centers, power generation, defense, and reshoring continue supporting U.S. corporate revenues and earnings, while equity-market breadth has improved materially. The TIC data suggest overseas investors increasingly prefer exposure to that growth rather than the duration associated with financing the federal balance sheet.

That is constructive for U.S. equities because persistent foreign demand provides another source of marginal capital supporting asset prices. It also helps explain why the equity market has remained resilient despite historically elevated long-term yields. The United States continues attracting enormous amounts of overseas capital, but the destination of that capital increasingly matters. Foreign investors can remain extremely bullish on American assets while simultaneously becoming less willing to own Treasuries at prevailing yields.

There is another side to that trade, however, and the recent behavior of the dollar makes it increasingly relevant. Following Treasury's buyback announcement, long yields initially fell before beginning to retrace higher. The dollar experienced a much sharper decline toward 98 and, importantly, has not recovered to the same degree. That matters because a foreign investor's return on U.S. equities is not simply the return of the underlying stock market. For an unhedged investor, it is the equity return combined with the change in the dollar relative to the investor's home currency.

A weaker dollar therefore reduces the home-currency return earned by foreign holders of U.S. equities. BIS research has highlighted that a meaningful portion of foreign equity exposure is held without full currency hedging, leaving overseas investors directly exposed to dollar movements. That creates an important asymmetry around the record foreign equity inflows accumulated over the past year. A rising U.S. equity market combined with a stable or stronger dollar creates an extremely attractive return for foreign investors. A weakening dollar can begin offsetting those gains even if the S&P 500 itself continues moving higher.

This does not mean a modest dollar decline automatically triggers foreign equity selling. Currency weakness can coexist with continued overseas inflows when U.S. earnings growth and relative equity performance remain sufficiently attractive. The risk emerges if dollar depreciation becomes large enough to materially erode those returns at the same time equity momentum slows. At that point, foreign investors would be confronting losses or weaker returns on the currency side precisely after accumulating historically large exposure to U.S. equities.

Positioning makes that possibility more important. Dollar positioning remains near the upper end of its recent historical range even after beginning to roll over, leaving substantial exposure available to unwind if lower policy expectations and attempts to relieve pressure on long-term yields continue undermining the currency. The same dollar decline that benefits metals, miners, Emerging Markets, and other dollar-sensitive assets can therefore eventually become a headwind for the enormous pool of foreign capital already invested in U.S. equities.

This brings us back to the U.S. Net International Investment Position, which remains deeply negative at roughly $27 trillion. The United States has accumulated an enormous external liability because foreigners own substantially more U.S. assets than Americans own foreign assets. That imbalance has been sustainable because the United States continues attracting global capital through deep financial markets, strong corporate profitability, reserve-currency status, and superior returns across many U.S. assets. Record foreign equity buying demonstrates that this attraction remains firmly intact.

But a deeply negative NIIP also means U.S. asset prices are increasingly exposed to the preferences of foreign capital. When overseas investors favor equities over Treasuries, that preference supports stocks while potentially increasing pressure on long-duration yields. If the dollar subsequently weakens enough to reduce the attractiveness of those equity holdings, the same capital that currently provides an important bid beneath the market can become more sensitive to relative returns elsewhere.

The TIC data therefore reinforce two very different messages simultaneously. The constructive message is that foreign investors continue demonstrating extraordinary confidence in U.S. corporate assets. The less comfortable message is that they are increasingly reluctant to finance the U.S. government at prevailing long-term yields, while their record equity exposure introduces greater sensitivity to a sustained decline in the dollar.

Foreign capital is not leaving the United States.

It is choosing where within the United States it wants to be.

Right now, that choice is overwhelmingly equities over duration. The sustainability of that preference increasingly depends on whether U.S. earnings growth remains strong enough to compensate foreign investors for the currency risk they are taking along the way.

Labor Breadth

Payroll Weakness Is Rising, but Not Yet Synchronized

Meanwhile, the latest state-level employment data continue to provide a more constructive signal than the weakness in recent headline payroll reports would suggest. One of the breadth measures we have built to monitor the labor cycle is the percentage of states experiencing year-over-year declines in payroll employment. Historically, recessions have not simply been characterized by weaker national payroll growth. Employment weakness becomes increasingly synchronized geographically, with the percentage of states losing jobs eventually moving well above 50% and, during deeper contractions, approaching 100%. Earlier this year, that measure briefly moved above 60%, reaching a level that deserved attention. Since then, however, the deterioration has reversed sharply. Only about 25.5% of states are now experiencing lower payroll employment than one year ago, meaning roughly three-quarters of the country continues to employ more workers than it did twelve months earlier.

That reinforces the distinction we have made throughout recent reports between a labor market experiencing slower hiring and one entering a broad firing cycle. Claims continue telling a similar story, with Initial Jobless Claims around 206K this week, a level that remains difficult to reconcile with widespread labor-market stress. Payroll growth has slowed, revisions have been negative, job openings have normalized, and the quits rate has fallen, but employers still are not reducing existing headcount aggressively enough to produce the geographic deterioration historically associated with recession. For the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, that leaves considerably more stability than the negative July payroll print alone would imply.

The more interesting weakness is increasingly appearing through the consumer rather than outright employment. Walmart's latest results provide a useful example. U.S. comparable sales increased just 2.6%, the slowest pace in six years and below expectations, while store-traffic growth slowed to 1.5% from 3% in the prior quarter. Management specifically highlighted the trade-offs consumers are making as gasoline prices rise. That fits directly with the affordability framework discussed in our previous report. Consumers remain employed, but the cumulative increase in housing, food, insurance, energy, and financing costs continues consuming a larger share of household cash flow, particularly across the lower half of the K-shaped economy.

The Walmart internals also illustrate why consumer weakness does not necessarily translate one-for-one into corporate earnings weakness. E-commerce grew roughly 24%, Walmart Connect advertising increased more than 40%, and membership revenue remained strong. Scale, logistics, digital distribution, advertising, and recurring membership revenue allow a dominant platform to protect earnings even when the household shopping inside that platform becomes more price sensitive. The consumer can therefore deteriorate at the margin while the company serving that consumer remains fundamentally resilient. That is another expression of the bifurcation we continue seeing throughout the economy: household cash-flow sensitivity can worsen without immediately producing the corporate earnings contraction normally associated with recession.

This is why the next phase of the cycle may depend less on whether people currently have jobs and more on what their income can actually purchase. Employment remains broad enough geographically to sustain aggregate labor income, but affordability pressure is forcing consumers to make increasingly visible trade-offs. If employment remains intact while energy prices moderate and real wage growth gradually repairs purchasing power, consumption can continue muddling through. If oil remains elevated and households begin reducing discretionary spending more aggressively, the economy can experience meaningful consumer weakness without first producing the traditional unemployment shock.

That tension becomes particularly important when considering new work from the San Francisco Fed estimating the medium-run real natural rate of interest, or r-star, near 1.5%. R-star is the theoretical real interest rate consistent with an economy operating around potential without generating either accelerating inflation or contraction. The estimate is inherently uncertain and should not be treated as an observable policy target, but it provides a useful framework for thinking about how restrictive current policy actually is. With the nominal funds rate at 3.50% to 3.75% and inflation near 3%, the ex-post real policy rate sits around 0.50% to 0.75%, below that 1.5% estimate. Under that framework, monetary policy may not be particularly restrictive in aggregate even though specific portions of the economy experience financial conditions as extremely restrictive.

That apparent contradiction is actually consistent with much of the data discussed throughout our recent work. Housing and other long-duration sectors face mortgage rates and market-based financing costs tied to a long end of the Treasury curve sitting near multi-decade highs. Lower-income consumers face elevated credit-card, auto, and other borrowing costs while simultaneously absorbing higher food and energy prices. Yet the AI-linked investment economy continues deploying extraordinary amounts of capital, manufacturing New Orders remain strong, corporate earnings are resilient, and equity prices remain elevated. An aggregate estimate of monetary accommodation can therefore coexist with severe restraint across the specific sectors most dependent on market-based borrowing.

This is also why simply raising the policy rate again would be an unusually blunt solution to the current inflation problem. Higher rates do not increase the supply of oil, resolve disruptions associated with Iran, build additional housing, or immediately expand the semiconductor, power, and electrical-equipment capacity being strained by AI investment. They would instead transmit most aggressively into precisely the rate-sensitive areas already experiencing the greatest pressure. Housing would become less affordable, consumer financing costs would increase further, and small businesses dependent on floating-rate credit would absorb another increase in their cost of capital.

There is, however, another side to the argument. The pressure at the long end increasingly reflects questions surrounding inflation credibility and term premium rather than simply expectations for the next Fed decision. If markets conclude that the Federal Reserve is unwilling to respond to persistent inflation because portions of the economy are rate sensitive, investors may demand even greater compensation for holding long-duration Treasuries. Counterintuitively, a modest Fed hike could therefore tighten the front end while helping stabilize the long end if investors interpret the move as evidence that policymakers remain committed to price stability. In that scenario, the credibility channel could partially offset the mechanical tightening channel by reducing inflation risk premium farther out the curve.

That does not make another hike the obvious policy choice. It illustrates how complicated the reaction function has become. The labor market is cooling but remains geographically broad. The consumer is becoming more price sensitive but has not stopped spending. Manufacturing and AI-related investment remain strong. Inflation is moderating underneath energy volatility, yet oil and selected capital inputs continue generating supply-driven pressure. Meanwhile, the long end is increasingly demanding compensation for fiscal, inflation, and duration risk.

The Fed is therefore confronting an economy where the areas most capable of absorbing higher rates may not be the areas creating the inflation problem, while the areas most vulnerable to higher rates are already struggling with affordability. That is why the next policy decision cannot be reduced to whether payrolls are weak or CPI is above target. The more important question is whether maintaining credibility requires additional restraint when the labor market remains fundamentally intact, or whether the tightening already embedded in long-term yields is sufficient to prevent the remaining inflation pressure from becoming entrenched.

For now, the state employment data argue that the Fed still has time to make that decision. The firing cycle has not arrived. But the Walmart data are a reminder that households do not need to lose their jobs before higher prices and financing costs begin changing behavior. The labor market remains the cushion. The consumer's ability to absorb additional pressure is increasingly the constraint.

Investment Split

Manufacturing Is Accelerating Where Capital Is Flowing

Manufacturing continues to represent one of the strongest areas of the U.S. economy and, importantly, the latest Philadelphia Fed survey suggests the improvement may still be accelerating. The current General Activity Index jumped to 47.4, while New Orders rose to 30.1 and Employment increased to 27.9. Those readings are already constructive on their own, but the six-month expectations were considerably more striking. Future General Activity surged to 73.6, its highest reading since August 1983, while Future New Orders reached 66.0, Future Shipments climbed to 63.5, and expected Employment rose to 35.4. Perhaps most importantly for the broader framework we have developed throughout this report, expected capital expenditures increased to 48.2, the strongest reading in 53 years.

The strength in forward capital spending fits directly with the increasingly bifurcated economy discussed above. Housing, commercial real estate, and portions of the consumer remain constrained by elevated long-term borrowing costs, while the capital-intensive side of the economy continues operating under an entirely different set of conditions. AI infrastructure, data centers, semiconductor capacity, power generation, electrical equipment, defense, and reshoring continue attracting enormous amounts of capital despite restrictive real yields. Rather than responding to higher rates by pulling back, many of these industries are effectively being forced to invest because demand for compute, power, and physical infrastructure continues growing faster than existing capacity.

This is why the Future Capex reading deserves particular attention. Survey expectations can be volatile and should not be treated as equivalent to realized spending, but a 53-year high is difficult to dismiss. The next confirmation should come from the hard data, particularly Nondefense Capital Goods Orders excluding Aircraft and the corresponding shipments series. If those measures begin accelerating alongside the survey, it would provide considerably stronger evidence that the manufacturing recovery is transitioning from an improvement in sentiment toward another leg higher in actual capital formation.

The New Orders data tell a similar story. Philly Fed Future New Orders at 66.0 are now signaling considerably stronger demand over the next six months, while ISM Manufacturing New Orders already sit at 56.7 and firmly in expansion territory. Historically, orders sit near the front of the industrial cycle because today's orders become tomorrow's production, shipments, revenues, capital expenditures, and eventually employment. The combination therefore argues against interpreting the recent deterioration in aggregate payroll growth as evidence that the entire business cycle is rolling over. Labor is cooling, but one of the most forward-looking portions of the private economy is simultaneously accelerating.

This also reinforces the shift in payroll composition discussed earlier. Government employment has moved into contraction while private payroll growth has begun stabilizing, and the manufacturing surveys suggest there is a plausible mechanism for that improvement to continue. If stronger orders translate into higher production and capital spending, manufacturers, construction companies, engineering firms, and the broader physical infrastructure ecosystem will eventually require additional labor. The economy does not need to return to the extraordinary payroll growth of the reopening period to remain healthy. It simply needs private-sector investment to generate enough income and employment to offset the fading government impulse and weakness across rate-sensitive industries.

The complication is that the same data supporting the growth outlook also reinforce the Fed's concern that the final stage of disinflation may prove difficult. Future Prices Paid increased to 62.9 while Future Prices Received rose to 59.8. Manufacturers are therefore expecting stronger activity, stronger orders, more hiring, substantially more capital spending, and greater pricing pressure simultaneously. That is not a recessionary configuration, but neither is it an obviously dovish one.

This connects directly to the capacity problem discussed previously. Aggregate U.S. Capacity Utilization remains only 76.3%, roughly three percentage points below its long-run average, suggesting considerable slack when the economy is viewed as a single production system. But AI investment is not demanding the average unit of U.S. capacity. It is concentrated within semiconductors, memory, servers, electrical equipment, power generation, steel, cooling systems, data-center construction, software, and specialized labor. Real Intellectual Property investment is already growing at an 8.8% annualized rate, while Capital Goods Import Prices are up 6.7% year over year. The economy can therefore possess substantial aggregate slack while simultaneously experiencing shortages and inflation within the specific capacity everyone suddenly needs.

That increasingly looks like the central tension confronting the Federal Reserve. The labor market is cooling enough to reduce the probability of a traditional wage-price spiral, but the capital spending cycle is strong enough to keep nominal growth and selected input prices elevated. The July FOMC minutes showed that policymakers remain sensitive to exactly that possibility, with a meaningful hawkish constituency still willing to consider additional tightening if inflation fails to moderate. The Philadelphia Fed survey provides ammunition for that side of the debate because businesses are not describing an economy preparing for contraction. They are describing one preparing to invest aggressively.

At the same time, the Treasury market is imposing its own form of restraint. Term premium remains near the 97th percentile of its post-2010 distribution, long-term yields remain historically elevated, foreign investors are increasingly favoring U.S. equities over long-duration Treasuries, and Treasury has already demonstrated sensitivity to the economic consequences of allowing the long end to move materially higher. This creates an unusual policy conflict. The administration wants relief from long-term yields because housing and other rate-sensitive portions of the economy are struggling, while the manufacturing and AI investment cycles remain strong enough that the Federal Reserve cannot simply validate dramatically easier financial conditions without considering the inflation consequences.

The result is an economy increasingly operating through two different channels. The traditional credit-sensitive economy is asking for lower rates. The capital-intensive investment economy is behaving as though rates are barely restrictive at all. That helps explain why long-term yields remain difficult to suppress despite softer aggregate employment data. Investors are not simply pricing the next Fed meeting. They are pricing an economy where fiscal deficits remain large, capital spending remains extraordinary, manufacturing demand is accelerating, and the industries receiving the most investment are already encountering supply constraints.

For markets, that distinction remains constructive for the earnings cycle but complicated for duration. Stronger manufacturing orders and record capital-spending intentions provide another reason corporate earnings and private investment can remain resilient even as portions of the consumer weaken. But the same strength makes a sustained collapse in long-term yields more difficult unless inflation moderates independently. This may ultimately be why equities continue attracting foreign capital while Treasuries struggle to generate the same demand. Investors increasingly want exposure to the companies receiving the capital rather than the duration financing the broader system.

The Philadelphia Fed survey therefore fits cleanly into the narrative developed throughout this report. The labor market has cooled without producing a firing cycle. The consumer remains constrained by affordability. Housing continues absorbing the impact of elevated long rates. Yet manufacturing, AI infrastructure, and capital spending continue accelerating in the opposite direction. The next question is whether that investment boom expands productive capacity quickly enough to become the disinflationary productivity story its proponents expect, or whether demand continues outrunning supply and keeps nominal growth, input prices, and term premium elevated along the way.

For now, the survey is sending a clear message: the economy may be cooling where rates matter most, but it is still accelerating where capital is flowing fastest.

Housing Constraint

Housing Is Weak, but Construction Labor Has Not Broken

Housing remains the clearest negative signal within an otherwise increasingly resilient private investment cycle. July Housing Starts fell 12.4% month over month to a 1.239 million annualized pace, materially below the 1.350 million expected, while June was revised modestly lower to 1.415 million. Starts are now down 13.5% from one year ago, and the weakness was particularly pronounced in the single-family market, where starts fell 9.9% to 808K, the weakest pace since November 2022 and 15.7% below July 2025 levels. Monthly housing data are notoriously volatile and the Census confidence intervals around the single-family data remain wide, but the decline in total starts was large enough to reinforce what the broader housing data have been telling us for some time: elevated financing costs continue materially restraining residential construction.

The permit data were considerably better and prevent us from interpreting the report as a collapse in the housing pipeline. Total Building Permits increased 5.0% to 1.443 million, comfortably above expectations, while Single-Family Permits rose 2.5% to 894K. The distinction between permits and starts is important. Permits represent the intention and legal ability to build, while starts represent the point where developers actually commit capital and begin construction. The fact that permits are holding up while starts weaken suggests builders have not abandoned future projects, but they remain reluctant to convert that pipeline into actual construction under current financing and demand conditions.

That hesitation makes sense when placed alongside the long-rate discussion above. The 30-year Treasury yield recently moved above 5%, term premium remains near the 97th percentile of its post-2010 distribution, and mortgage rates continue sitting at levels that leave the monthly payment on a home incompatible with incomes for a large portion of prospective buyers. The Fed can stop hiking, and Treasury can attempt to improve functioning at the long end, but neither development automatically produces the decline in mortgage rates required to materially change housing affordability. As long as real yields and term premium keep long-term borrowing costs elevated, residential construction remains one of the clearest channels through which restrictive financial conditions are reaching the real economy.

Pending Home Sales reinforce that interpretation from the demand side. Contracts fell another 2.3% month over month following the 5.4% decline in June, pushing the Pending Home Sales Index down to 71.2, its lowest level since January. All four major regions declined sequentially and pending transactions are now down 2.2% from one year ago. That tells us builders are not simply responding to higher financing costs on their own balance sheets. The end buyer remains constrained as well. Elevated home prices combined with mortgage rates near multi-year highs continue suppressing the transaction volume required to justify a meaningful acceleration in new construction.

The chart below puts the weakness into a broader business-cycle context by pairing Housing Starts and Building Permits with Construction Employment. Historically, starts and permits lead construction payrolls because builders first respond to weaker demand by reducing future projects. Employment adjusts later as projects already underway are completed, backlogs decline, and contractors eventually determine that the slowdown is persistent enough to reduce headcount. That sequencing is one reason housing has historically been such a useful leading indicator around economic turning points.

What makes the current cycle so unusual is that the normal transmission mechanism has largely broken down. Housing Starts and Permits have been stagnant to lower for several years, yet Construction Employment continues making new highs near 8.34 million workers. In prior cycles, particularly ahead of the Global Financial Crisis, sustained deterioration in residential construction eventually produced a corresponding decline in construction payrolls. Today, the labor side has moved almost completely in the opposite direction.

The explanation increasingly comes back to the bifurcation running through this entire report. Residential construction is weak, but construction itself is not simply a housing industry. The enormous capital spending cycle surrounding data centers, semiconductor facilities, power generation, electrical infrastructure, manufacturing reshoring, defense, and AI-related infrastructure is creating demand for many of the same electricians, engineers, specialty contractors, and construction workers that historically would have been more exposed to the residential cycle. Weakness in the rate-sensitive old economy is therefore being offset by extraordinary investment across the capital-intensive new economy.

This helps reconcile several seemingly contradictory data points. Housing Starts are down 13.5% year over year while Philly Fed Future Capital Expenditures have reached their highest level in 53 years. Residential builders are pulling back while manufacturers report rapidly improving New Orders and expectations for future activity. Mortgage-sensitive households are constrained while hyperscalers and infrastructure developers continue committing enormous amounts of capital regardless of prevailing interest rates. These are not necessarily conflicting signals. They are increasingly two different investment cycles occurring simultaneously within the same economy.

Construction Employment sits directly between those two cycles and may therefore become one of the more important confirmation indicators from here. As long as nonresidential investment remains strong enough to absorb workers displaced or underutilized by residential weakness, the housing downturn can remain largely sector-specific. It will weigh on residential investment, housing turnover, affordability, and the associated consumer ecosystem without necessarily becoming the catalyst for a broader recession.

The risk emerges if that offset begins weakening. Starts and permits have already provided the traditional early warning. If AI-related and nonresidential capital spending eventually slows and Construction Employment begins following residential activity lower, the housing weakness would start transmitting through labor income and consumption in a much more conventional cyclical fashion. That would represent a materially different macro signal than weak starts alone.

For now, however, the divergence remains intact. Housing is clearly restrictive, but construction employment is not. Residential investment is contracting while broader capital investment remains exceptionally strong. This is precisely why the current economy has been able to withstand a level of long-term interest rates that historically would have produced considerably greater damage.

It also explains the increasingly difficult position facing policymakers. Lower long-term yields would provide meaningful relief to housing and other rate-sensitive areas, but easier financial conditions would arrive while the AI and manufacturing investment cycle is already accelerating and encountering pockets of capacity pressure. Higher rates, meanwhile, would disproportionately attack housing and the consumer without necessarily addressing the supply-driven inflation emerging across energy and AI-linked capital goods.

Housing therefore remains the clearest evidence that monetary restraint is working somewhere. The broader question is whether policymakers can provide enough relief to prevent that weakness from spreading without simultaneously adding fuel to the parts of the economy that remain extraordinarily strong. For now, the answer has come from the private economy itself: residential construction is contracting, but the capital spending boom elsewhere continues filling the gap.

Bottom Line

Two Economies Are Operating Side by Side

The broader message from this week's data is that the economy is not moving toward a conventional late-cycle slowdown where tighter policy progressively weakens every major component of demand at the same time. Instead, the cycle is becoming increasingly bifurcated. Housing, real estate, and portions of the consumer remain constrained by borrowing costs and affordability, while AI infrastructure, semiconductors, data centers, power, defense, and related manufacturing investment continue expanding at rates that appear remarkably insensitive to the same cost of capital. That divergence is allowing headline GDP, industrial activity, employment, and corporate earnings to remain considerably more resilient than traditional rate-sensitive leading indicators would normally imply.

This helps reconcile what otherwise looks like a contradictory macro environment. Growth is slowing at the margin and labor demand has cooled, but the firing cycle has not arrived. Housing is clearly restrictive, yet Construction Employment remains near record highs because nonresidential investment continues absorbing labor. The consumer is becoming increasingly sensitive to higher prices, particularly energy and financing costs, but aggregate spending and corporate earnings remain supported by employment, asset prices, and the upper half of the K. At the same time, manufacturing New Orders are accelerating and capital-spending intentions have reached extraordinary levels. The economy is therefore experiencing meaningful weakness without yet producing the synchronization across sectors that normally turns weakness into recession.

The complication is that this resilience comes with an inflation cost. The AI investment boom may ultimately prove enormously productive, but the infrastructure required to realize those productivity gains must be built first. That process is competing for a finite supply of semiconductors, memory, power, electrical equipment, industrial machinery, commodities, construction capacity, and specialized labor. Aggregate capacity utilization can remain subdued while the specific capacity receiving hundreds of billions of dollars in incremental demand becomes scarce. The result is an economy where traditional labor inflation is moderating at the same time a new capital-intensive source of price pressure is developing elsewhere.

That leaves policymakers confronting an unusually difficult trade-off. The areas most vulnerable to additional tightening are increasingly not the areas responsible for the remaining inflation pressure. Another rate hike would transmit quickly into housing, consumer credit, small businesses, and other rate-sensitive sectors, while doing relatively little to produce more oil, electricity, transformers, semiconductors, or data-center capacity. Yet easing aggressively is equally difficult while manufacturing accelerates, AI capex remains extraordinary, oil stays elevated, and underlying inflation remains above target. The Fed therefore has little reason to rush in either direction.

The long end of the Treasury curve has become the pressure valve for that uncertainty. Term premium near the 97th percentile tells us investors increasingly want compensation not simply for the expected path of Fed policy, but for fiscal deficits, inflation uncertainty, Treasury supply, geopolitical risk, and the possibility that nominal growth remains structurally stronger than expected. Treasury's decision to increase long-duration buybacks shows that policymakers are becoming uncomfortable with the economic consequences of allowing that adjustment to occur entirely through higher yields. But the relatively small size of those operations compared with the government's financing requirement means they can improve market functioning without resolving the underlying compensation problem.

Foreign capital flows reinforce that tension. Overseas investors are not abandoning the United States. Record equity purchases suggest almost the opposite. They are increasingly choosing exposure to U.S. corporate growth over the long-duration government debt financing the system. That remains supportive for equities, but it also means the marginal Treasury buyer may require a higher yield. With the U.S. Net International Investment Position deeply negative, that preference matters increasingly for both asset prices and the currency.

This is where the recent weakness in the dollar and strength across hard assets become particularly interesting. Gold and miners have rallied sharply even with real yields remaining historically elevated, while the dollar has failed to recover alongside the rebound in long Treasury yields. Conventional macro relationships would normally struggle to produce that combination. One interpretation is that markets are beginning to assign some probability to policymakers resisting a full adjustment in sovereign financing costs through higher nominal yields. If the long end becomes politically or economically intolerable and policymakers increasingly lean against it, some portion of the adjustment may instead appear through a weaker currency and higher hard-asset risk premia.

That does not make this a fiscal or financial crisis. Credit markets are not signaling systemic stress, volatility remains contained, equity breadth remains healthy, and foreign investors continue purchasing U.S. corporate assets aggressively. Those indicators matter because they remain important vetoes on the more bearish interpretation. For now, the evidence is more consistent with a valuation and discount-rate shock carrying an increasingly important fiscal-credibility component than with a breakdown in the financial system.

The emerging regime therefore looks increasingly distinct:

Rate-sensitive old economy: housing, real estate, and portions of the consumer remain constrained.

Capital-intensive new economy: AI infrastructure, semiconductors, data centers, power, defense, and manufacturing remain resilient to accelerating.

That split can persist longer than traditional cycle analysis would suggest because the strength of the second group continues offsetting weakness in the first. But it also leaves less room for policy error. Suppressing long rates too aggressively risks adding liquidity to the very investment cycle already creating pockets of inflation. Allowing yields to clear materially higher risks eventually overwhelming housing, the consumer, and other rate-sensitive sectors. Tightening the front end may reinforce Fed credibility, but it simultaneously increases pressure on the weakest portions of the economy.

For now, the economy continues navigating that narrow path. Growth is slowing without contracting, labor is cooling without broad layoffs, housing is weak without pulling Construction Employment lower, and manufacturing is accelerating despite historically restrictive long-term borrowing costs. The market is still treating those divergences as manageable.

The signal that would change our view is not weakness in any one of these areas. It would be convergence. If housing weakness finally pulls Construction Employment lower, consumer pressure turns into broader spending contraction, manufacturing orders roll over, credit spreads widen, and equity breadth deteriorates simultaneously, the separate pockets of stress would finally become one business-cycle downturn. Until then, the more useful framework is not to ask whether the economy is strong or weak. It is to recognize that two very different economies are currently operating side by side, and the interaction between them is increasingly determining the path of inflation, policy, yields, the dollar, and asset prices.
